sections.h2: What does the Medina County Recorder do?
sections.html:
The Medina County Recorder keeps the permanent land records for the county: every deed, mortgage, easement and similar paper that conveys or encumbers land. The office is at 144 N. Broadway Street, Room 117, in the city of Medina, and the main number is 330-725-9782. A document search page on the recorder's website lets you look up recorded deeds and mortgages from home.

Staff accept documents, index them and store them in archival form. They do not decide who owns a house. For a seller, the recorder's index is where a title company confirms the chain of owners and finds any open mortgage that must be released at closing.

sections.h2: What will the Medina County Recorder charge to file a deed?
sections.html:
The recorder's fee page lists $34 for the first two pages of a deed, $8 for each added page and $4 for each marginal notation. The office says half of that goes to the basic recording fee and half to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund, which matches section 317.32 of the Ohio Revised Code.

Medina County Recorder fees as printed on the recorder's fee page
ItemFee
First two pages (deeds, mortgages, easements, land contracts, leases)$34
Each additional page$8
Each marginal notation$4
Mortgage or other release$4
Certified copy$2 per page plus $1 for the seal
Federal tax lien$5
Document that misses the state format rules (ORC 317.114)$20 extra
Veteran discharge papers (DD214)Free

State law lets a county add a document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars. The fee page does not mention one, so call the office before you mail a check and ask for the exact total for your page count.

sections.h2: Who collects the transfer charge on a Medina County sale?
sections.html:
The county auditor does, before the deed ever reaches the recorder. The auditor's page sets the real property conveyance fee at $3.00 per $1,000 of the sale price, rounding up to the next $100 when the price ends in a fraction of a hundred. A conveyance fee calculator on the auditor's site gives an estimate.

A regular sale goes in with DTE Form 100. A transfer that qualifies for an exemption goes in with DTE Form 100EX. The auditor's list of exemptions includes:

  • a gift between spouses, or between a parent and child;
  • a transfer to an heir or devisee, or to a surviving spouse;
  • a deed that corrects or confirms one already recorded;
  • a transfer under a court order that is not itself a sale;
  • a deed to the trustee of a trust the grantor can revoke.

Manufactured homes carry their own rate of $1.00 per $1,000. Ask the auditor which form fits your deed before the signing.

sections.h2: Which county offices does a Medina County house sale touch?
sections.html:
A sale usually moves through three counters in the county seat, and the order matters. Getting it backward costs a few days.

  • Auditor: receives the statement of value and collects the conveyance fee.
  • Recorder: records the endorsed deed, any mortgage release and any affidavit.
  • Treasurer: holds the real estate tax payoff. Your title company will want the tax payoff figure, which comes from the county treasurer.

Title companies, lenders and attorneys can skip the trip by e-recording. The recorder lists three approved vendors, Simplifile, ePN and CSC eRecording Solutions, plus File and Go for notices of commencement. Each filer makes one ACH payment per day no matter how many documents go in, so there is no check written for the wrong amount.

sections.h2: What kind of county is Medina County?
sections.html:
Medina County covers 423 square miles in northeast Ohio and borders Cuyahoga, Summit, Wayne, Ashland and Lorain counties. According to Wikipedia, it was created in 1812, organized in 1818 and sits in the old Connecticut Western Reserve. It belongs to the Cleveland metropolitan area, although its southeastern corner is part of the Akron urban area.

Medina is the seat of government and Brunswick is the biggest city. Wadsworth is a city too, and Rittman reaches in from the south. Sharon Center and Valley City are census-designated places. The Medina County Park District, started in 1965, manages 6,353 acres across 18 parks and trails.

Westfield Insurance led the county's list of employers in 2020 with 2,040 workers, followed by the Cleveland Clinic Medina Hospital at 1,431 and county government at 1,365.

sections.h2: Which papers from a Medina County sale go through the recorder?
sections.html:
The fee page names the documents the office handles at the standard rate, and the list shows how varied a house transfer can be. Most Medina County sellers will meet only a few of them.

  • Warranty deeds, quit claim deeds and survivorship deeds.
  • Sheriff's deeds, which close out a foreclosure sale.
  • Mortgages, mortgage releases, assignments and subordinations.
  • Affidavits, powers of attorney and various trust documents.
  • Land contracts, leases and easements.

An inherited house often needs an affidavit or certificate alongside the deed. A house with a lender needs a release recorded after payoff, which carries the $4 release fee. Each paper is priced separately by page count, so a closing with a deed, a release and an affidavit produces three charges.

sections.h2: What makes a Medina County deed easy to record?
sections.html:
Ohio's standardization law, ORC 317.114, took effect July 1, 2009, and the recorder's fee page repeats it: a document that does not meet the requirements can be charged an extra $20. A clean deed avoids that charge and avoids a call back from the office.

Have the deed prepared by someone who knows Ohio's format and legal description rules, and confirm the page total before you pay. The county's website directs questions to the office at 330-725-9782. The Medina County Auditor also posts conveyance forms and a sales report, which show what nearby parcels sold for and help a seller check the figure going on the statement of value.

sections.h2: How big is the Medina County housing market?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table credits Medina County with 185,025 people as of July 2025. Its housing rows paint a prosperous, owner-heavy county.

  • Eight in ten homes (80.3 percent) are lived in by their owners, across 73,086 households.
  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $287,000.
  • Homeowners with a mortgage report $1,726 a month in costs; those without report $650.
  • Renters pay a median $1,143 in gross rent.
  • Household income reaches $94,968 at the median.
  • The county counted 77,727 housing units and issued 430 building permits during 2025.

Because so many households own, most recorded deeds here are ordinary owner-to-owner sales. Rental and inherited houses make up the rest.

sections.h2: How can a Medina County owner guard against deed fraud?
sections.html:
A free Property Fraud Alert comes with the office. Sign up through the recorder's website, and the automated system sends an email or phone alert whenever a transaction involving your property is recorded. The idea is to catch a forged deed early. The office at 330-725-9782 can help with the sign-up.

Veterans can record a DD214 at no cost, and the office issues a free Veteran's Identification Card once the discharge is on file. Recording the paper creates a certified source if the original is ever lost.

faqs.q: Where is the Medina County Recorder's office?
faqs.a: It is at 144 N. Broadway Street, Room 117, Medina, Ohio 44256. The office phone is 330-725-9782. Call before you go to confirm hours and the total fee for your document.

faqs.q: What are the recording fees in Medina County?
faqs.a: The fee page prints $34 up to two pages and $8 per page beyond. A document that fails the state formatting rules draws an extra $20. Ask the office whether the optional preservation surcharge applies to your filing.

faqs.q: Does the recorder charge the real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: No. The county auditor collects the conveyance fee, which the auditor's page sets at $3.00 per $1,000 of the sale price. Exempt transfers use DTE Form 100EX and pay no conveyance fee.

faqs.q: Can lenders and title agents e-record Medina County deeds?
faqs.a: Yes, through Simplifile, ePN or CSC eRecording Solutions, all under contract with the office. Homeowners generally do not e-record on their own, so ask your closing agent.

faqs.q: Can Medina County owners get an alert when a document hits their property record?
faqs.a: Yes. The recorder runs a free Property Fraud Alert program that sends an email or phone notice when a transaction involving your property is recorded.
